In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of chromosome segregation in the mouse and the influence of the karyotype of sperm on fertilizing competence.
the effects of aneuploid spermatozoa on the fertilizing capacity of male mice.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sperm with chromosomal aberrations are not necessarily infertile, but rather that the fertility of such sperm is variable and depends upon the nature and extent of the aberration as well as the age of the sperm.

, in the mouse, the sperm of a heterozygote for a balanced translocation may be capable of fertilization and of contributing to the zygote complement, even if aneuploid, provided that the aneuploids are not nullisomics for the chromosomes of the Robertsonian translocation.

sperm with chromosomal anomalies can be fertilizing competent and that the effect of such anomalies on fertilizing ability depends on the chromosomes involved and on the storage period in the reproductive tract.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 2:2 meiotic segregation products are equifrequent, but the 3:1 products are infrequent in the mouse.
, in general, the 2:2 meiotic segregants are the predominant types of sperm karyotypes in the male and are capable of fertilizing in vitro.

the sperm complement is not a random selection of meiotic segregants, that sperm with chromosomal anomalies are not functionally impaired, that the fertilization competence of sperm is dependent on the prior storage time in the male, and that the effect of chromosomal aneuploids on sperm function is specific for the particular chromosome(s) involved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sperm karyotype is a significant determinant of fertilizing competence.
, while sperm with aneuploidies can still fertilize oocytes, their ability to do so depends on the specific chromosomes involved.
